Theme

Time, the calendar & feasts · Conversation, family & daily routines

youth noun

the time of being young

also in my youth, when I was young, adolescence, teenage years, the teens

classical

Cic. Sen. 70: vēr enim tamquam adulēscentiam significat
Tac. Agr. 4.2: pueritiam adulēscentiamque trānsēgit
Traupman 410

adulēscentia, adulēscentiae f.

noun, first declension

youth, the years between boyhood and manhood

The age of the adulēscēns, which Lewis & Short put roughly from fifteen to thirty: after pueritia (see childhood) and before juventūs in the strict sense. The everyday word for one’s youth.

Other words

  • juventa, juventae f. — youth, the age of youth

    noun, first declension · also used · classical · Verg. A. 5.295: viridīque juventā (Lewis & Short); Ov. Met. 15.209: positō fervōre juventae

    (vōx plērumque poētica et post Augustum: Verg., Ov.; Liv.)

    Mostly post-Augustan for the classical juventūs (Lewis & Short).

  • juventūs, juventūtis f. — the age of youth (strictly from twenty to forty)

    noun, third declension · also used · classical · Sall. C. 5.2: ibique juventūtem suam exercuit (Lewis & Short)

    In this sense rare; far more often young people collectively (see youth, young people) (Lewis & Short).

Examples

  • vēr enim tamquam adulēscentiam significat ostenditque frūctūs futūrōs

    for spring stands for youth, as it were, and shows the fruit to comeCic. Sen. 70

  • frūctuōsior est adulēscentia līberōrum, sed īnfantia dulcior

    children’s youth bears more fruit, but their infancy is sweeterSen. Ep. 9.7

  • in hujus sinū indulgentiāque ēducātus per omnem honestārum artium cultum pueritiam adulēscentiamque trānsēgit

    brought up in her lap and her loving care, he spent his childhood and youth in the study of every honourable artTac. Agr. 4.2

See also youth, childhood, young, life, old, generation.
